original_question: A positive integer is called a pseudo-prime of third kind if some nontrivial permutation of its decimal digits is prime. Among those numbers, are there infinitely many that are themselves prime?
target_in_paper: Item 83, "Pseudo-Primes of Third Kind": "Question: How many pseudo-primes of third kind are prime numbers? (We conjecture: an infinity)." ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the correct object (pseudo-primes of third kind), the key condition that a nontrivial digit permutation should be prime, and the intended infinitude question restricted to those members that are themselves prime. It is very close to the paper's official open problem. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
missing_details: The paper's exact target is item 83 specifically; it should not be broadened to first-kind or second-kind pseudo-primes. The nearby definitions of items 81 and 82 are part of the needed context. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The paper explicitly explains that "nontrivial" means a permutation "different from the identity permutation"; that clarification should be stated in a stand-alone version. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

For full precision, the permutation should be described as acting on digit positions in the ordinary decimal expansion of n. This matters because repeated digits can make a nonidentity permutation produce the same numeral; the listed term 11 shows that such cases are included. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The prose leaves the treatment of leading zeros implicit, but the displayed sequence contains terms such as 20 and 30, showing that permutations like 02 and 03 are read as the integers 2 and 3. A self-contained formulation should make that convention explicit. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))

The paper phrases the problem as an infinitude conjecture, not as a density or asymptotic-counting problem: "How many ... ? (We conjecture: an infinity)." The refined version should preserve exactly that scope. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
refined_question: In base 10, let n be a positive integer. Call n a pseudo-prime of third kind if some permutation of the positions of the digits in the decimal expansion of n, other than the identity permutation, yields a prime number when read as a decimal integer (so a leading zero may disappear). Are there infinitely many pseudo-primes of third kind that are themselves prime?
justification: The draft is aimed at the open problem in numbered item 83 on page 40, and the refined question keeps exactly that scope: positive integers in decimal notation, a nonidentity digit permutation producing a prime, and the conjectural infinitude of those members that are prime themselves. I did not broaden to item 81 (first kind, which allows the identity permutation), item 82 (second kind, which requires the original number to be composite), or to the analogous square/cube questions that follow. The introduction confirms that the paper is a collection of such sequence definitions and open questions. ([fs.unm.edu](https://fs.unm.edu/Sequences-book.pdf))
